Heat (Q)

 Home Physics Branches of physics Statistical physics Thermodynamics
OurBigBook.com Words: 13k Articles: 119
Heat is energy transferred across a thermodynamic system's boundary because of a temperature difference. It is measured in joules, like work and internal energy. A hot cup transfers heat to cooler surroundings; its temperature describes its state, while the transferred heat describes a process. The cup stores internal energy, rather than a substance called heat. [ref]
For a closed system with unchanged bulk kinetic energy and potential energy, choose Q>0 for heat entering and W>0 for work done by the system. The first law of thermodynamics gives
ΔU=Q−W,dU=δQ−δW.
(1)
Here U is the stored internal energy. For example, a sealed piston cylinder receiving 20kJ of heat and delivering 5kJ of work gains 15kJ of internal energy. A closed system retains its matter while exchanging energy; it need not be an isolated system. [ref]
Unlike internal energy, heat is not a state function: different paths between the same equilibrium states can transfer different Q, with compensating differences in work. The symbol δQ records this dependence on the path; there is no stored quantity whose difference is always Q. The two paths in first law of thermodynamics illustrate this directly. Supplied heat can raise temperature as sensible heat, change a phase fraction through latent heat, or help supply expansion work. Measuring temperature alone therefore does not determine transferred heat.
For a reversible thermodynamic process, δQrev​=TdS, where T is absolute temperature and S is entropy. This identification requires reversibility: an irreversible adiabatic process has Q=0 and can nevertheless increase entropy. Likewise Q=ΔH, with enthalpy H, requires the particular fixed-pressure conditions in enthalpy. These distinctions make heat useful as a precise boundary-transfer quantity in heat engines, refrigerators and heating calculations.
Historically, James Prescott Joule's paddle experiments showed that stirring water with input work could raise its temperature, helping establish conservation of energy. The lesson is still useful: a temperature rise can result from work even without incoming heat. [ref]

Lumped thermal model

Heat OurBigBook.com
A finite-dimensional energy-balance model assigning one representative temperature and heat capacity to each region. Thermal resistances represent the energy exchange between regions; internal spatial gradients are not resolved.

Sensible heat (Qsens​)

Words: 362
Heat OurBigBook.com
Sensible heat is transferred heat associated with a temperature change within a single thermodynamic phase. By contrast, latent heat can change the phase fraction while the temperature stays fixed during equilibrium phase coexistence. Neither name denotes an additional stored substance: both describe how transferred heat participates in a process.
For fixed mass m and composition, use the heat capacity appropriate to the heating constraint. Under the quasistatic process assumptions in heat capacity, with only pressure-volume work and unchanged bulk kinetic energy and potential energy, fixed-pressure heating gives
Qsens​=m∫T1​T2​​cp​(T)dT,Qsens​=mcp​(T2​−T1​)if cp​ is constant.
(2)
Here cp​ is specific heat capacity at constant pressure; fixed-volume heating instead uses specific heat capacity at constant volume cV​. A cooling step has negative Qsens​ with the sign convention in heat. A temperature difference has the same numerical value in units of the kelvin or degree Celsius. The integral follows by adding the small transfers δQ=mcp​(T)dT, rather than assuming a constant heat capacity.
As a stylized ice-to-water example for a fixed-composition closed system at fixed pressure 1atm, take m=0.5kg, an initial temperature of −10∘C, melting at 0∘C, and a final temperature of 20∘C. Assume constant specific heat capacity at constant pressure values cice​=2.1kJkg−1K−1 and cwater​=4.18kJkg−1K−1, and latent heat of fusion Lf​=334kJkg−1. These are stipulated, rounded model values; ignore the container and heat losses, retain all the material, and assume only pressure-volume work under the quasistatic process conditions above. The three steps are
Qice​Qmelt​Qwater​Qtotal​​=0.5×2.1×10=10.5kJ,=0.5×334=167kJ,=0.5×4.18×20=41.8kJ,=10.5+167+41.8=219.3kJ.​
(3)
Only the first and third terms are sensible heat; the middle term is latent heat. The plateau begins after 10.5kJ and ends after 177.5kJ of total supplied heat. At 94kJ total input, half the mass is liquid water and the temperature remains 0∘C. The equilibrium phase transition temperature depends on pressure; this example stipulates a single fixed pressure. [ref]
This split makes heating budgets easy to interpret: melting consumes 167/219.3≈76.2% of the supplied heat in this model despite causing no temperature rise. Within either single thermodynamic phase, the heating curve slope is dT/dQ=1/(mcp​); a larger heat capacity makes the slope shallower. A flat interval represents changing phase fraction, so it cannot be modeled by applying Q=mcp​ΔT across the phase transition. The complementary constructed example in latent heat tracks that phase fraction explicitly.

Heat transfer

Words: 1k Articles: 34
Heat OurBigBook.com
Heat transfer asks how quickly heat crosses a boundary and how the temperature varies along its path. Its principal mechanisms are thermal conduction, convection and thermal radiation. A warm wall can conduct heat through its interior while exchanging heat with moving air and emitting thermal radiation at its surfaces. Identifying these paths lets us estimate heating requirements and cooling times.
Distinguish the accumulated heat Q from its rate Q˙​=dQ/dt, a power measured in W. The heat flux q is the rate per unit area, measured in Wm−2: a uniform normal heat flux across area A gives Q˙​=Aq. The steady bar in thermal conduction carries q=400Wm−2 through A=0.01m2, hence Q˙​=4W; maintained for 60s, it transfers Q=240J. This distinction makes a surface's intensity and a whole object's heating load easy to compare.

A measure of how rapidly a material exchanges heat with another body in transient contact. Here k is thermal conductivity, ρ is mass density and cp​ is specific heat capacity. Perceived coldness at equal actual temperature can depend on this contact heat transfer rather than on an electronic Fermi temperature.

Radiative heat transfer (Pnet​=ϵσA(Ts4​−Te4​))

Words: 46
Heat transfer OurBigBook.com
Transfer of energy by thermal radiation. A diffuse grey surface of area A and emissivity ϵ completely enclosed by isothermal black surroundings has net outward power ϵσA(Ts4​−Te4​). This subtracts absorbed environmental radiation from emitted radiation. Other geometries require exchange factors; a gross emitted power is not a net cooling rate.

Convective heat transfer

Words: 39
Heat transfer OurBigBook.com
Energy transport by bulk fluid motion together with local thermal conduction. A prescribed adiabatic process profile constrains temperature but does not require zero convergence of this energy transport. A cloud held at a specified temperature can therefore have nonzero net radiative heating balanced by convection.

Heat transport

Words: 117 Articles: 1
Heat transfer OurBigBook.com
Transfer of thermal energy between regions. In a constant-property thermal Boussinesq approximation, the advective heat flux per unit area is ρ0​cp​Tu and transport across a section is its normal component integrated over that section. With zero net volume transport, adding a constant reference temperature does not change that integral. Otherwise the reference and the return-flow budget must be specified. Atmospheric energy transport also includes latent heat and gravitational potential energy.

Meridional heat transport (HT​=∫ρ0​cp​vTdA)

Words: 56
Heat transport OurBigBook.com
The component of heat transport crossing a latitude. A poleward transport is northward in the Northern Hemisphere and southward in the Southern Hemisphere. Equal and opposite volume transports can carry net heat when the poleward branch is warmer. For eddies, the corresponding transport is determined by the correlation of meridional velocity and temperature anomalies, closely related to eddy buoyancy flux in a thermal Boussinesq approximation.

Thermal insulation

Words: 94 Articles: 1
Heat transfer OurBigBook.com
thermal insulation reduces unwanted heat exchange. Conduction through supports, convection in gas and thermal radiation require different treatments. vacuum suppresses gas transport but leaves solid conduction and radiation; lowering thermal conductance also increases the temperature rise caused by a fixed internal heat load.

Thermal shield

Words: 60
Thermal insulation OurBigBook.com
A thermal shield reduces coupling to unwanted environmental temperature changes. Low-conductance supports and thermal insulation reduce heat transport, low-emissivity surfaces reduce thermal radiation, and a conducting inner enclosure can reduce temperature gradients. Combined with heat capacity these give a thermal low-pass response. Passive shielding cannot indefinitely reject a slow change in the entire environment and may increase the temperature rise from internal dissipation; active regulation addresses a different frequency range.

First-order thermal isolation (CδTs​˙​+GδTs​=GδTb​+δP)

Words: 104 Articles: 1
Heat transfer OurBigBook.com
A lumped sample of heat capacity C coupled by thermal conductance G to a bath has the displayed linearized energy balance. For constant internal power, the bath-to-sample temperature response is 1/(1+iωC/G). Insulation and heat capacity suppress rapid bath fluctuations but have unity static bath-to-sample gain. A steady power change shifts the sample by δP/G, so improved isolation increases self-heating sensitivity and equilibration time. The lumped approximation requires internal equilibration faster than the variations being modeled.

First-order thermal isolation OurBigBook.com
A first-order lumped thermal system relaxes exponentially with time constant C/G after a small bath-temperature or heating change. More complex systems have multiple thermal modes and need not have a single relaxation time.

A heat current is a rate of heat transfer across a specified boundary. Its sign requires a chosen direction; unlike heat flux, it is not a rate per unit area.

Heat-current relaxation time (τQ​)

Words: 55
Heat current OurBigBook.com
A heat-current relaxation time measures the decay of a departure from equilibrium carrying heat. It need not equal the momentum relaxation time or the time between arbitrary scattering events. In an isotropic degenerate-electron estimate, Ke​=ce​vF2​τQ​/3. Small-angle inelastic electron-phonon scattering can remove an excitation energy of order kB​T while barely changing the electron's velocity direction, thus relaxing heat more efficiently than charge flow.

Radiative cooling

Words: 671 Articles: 12
Heat transfer OurBigBook.com
A body loses internal energy by emitting thermal radiation faster than it absorbs radiation or receives other heating. In a gravitating gas this can remove pressure support and allow further contraction.

Compton cooling by the cosmic microwave background (tC​∝(1+z)−4/xe​)

Words: 67
Radiative cooling OurBigBook.com
Hot electrons can transfer energy to cosmic microwave background photons through Compton scattering. For a fixed electron fraction xe​ and electron temperature well above the radiation temperature, the optically thin gas cooling time scales approximately as (1+z)−4/xe​. Its volume loss scales with electron density, not with nH2​, because the radiation density is independent of local gas density. The process tends toward the radiation temperature; it heats rather than cools electrons colder than that radiation.

Dust thermal emission

Words: 44
Radiative cooling OurBigBook.com
Dust grains emit thermal radiation after absorbing energy from radiation or collisions. Collisions can transfer thermal energy from dense gas to grains, whose radiation then cools the gas. This channel requires dust and does not operate in strictly pristine hydrogen-helium material without prior enrichment.

Inverse Compton cooling (Pe​=4σT​cUγ​kB​(Te​−Tγ​)/(me​c2))

Words: 62
Radiative cooling OurBigBook.com
Thermal electrons can transfer energy to lower-energy radiation photons through Compton scattering. In the nonrelativistic Thomson regime, the net cooling power per electron is 4σT​cUγ​kB​(Te​−Tγ​)/(me​c2) for a blackbody photon bath. A sufficiently hot electron population therefore loses energy; a colder population is heated instead. The cosmic microwave background radiation energy density grows as (1+z)4, making this channel more important for high-redshift diffuse ionized gas.

Astrophysical cooling function (C=nH2​Λ(T))

Words: 471 Articles: 8
Radiative cooling OurBigBook.com
An astrophysical cooling function packages radiative losses of a plasma into a temperature-dependent coefficient. In the hydrogen-density-squared convention, the volume energy loss is nH2​Λ(T), so the coefficient has units ergcm3s−1. Its dependence on ionization state, chemical abundances and radiation field must be specified; a low-density collisional-equilibrium curve is not universal.
Electron-hydrogen normalization of the cooling function (C=ne​nH​ΛeH​)
Words: 56
Astrophysical cooling function OurBigBook.com
In an optically thin plasma, one convention defines the radiative cooling power per volume by C=ne​nH​ΛeH​(T), where nH​ counts hydrogen nuclei. A convention C=nH2​ΛHH​ instead has ΛHH​=(ne​/nH​)ΛeH​. Thus the tabulated functions differ even for the same gas. With total particle density n, a monatomic-gas radiative gas cooling time is 3nkB​T/(2C) when heating is negligible.[ref]
Molecular line cooling
Words: 53
Astrophysical cooling function OurBigBook.com
Radiation from rotational and vibrational transitions of molecules removes gas thermal energy. In primordial gas below the atomic threshold, molecular hydrogen is a principal coolant; hydrogen deuteride can matter in suitable chemical conditions. Molecular formation, photodissociation, optical depth and density-dependent level populations control the rate. This allows some small systems below the atomic virial temperature threshold to form stars.
Cooling suppression by photoionization
Words: 58
Astrophysical cooling function OurBigBook.com
Photoionization changes the ion population, often removing bound-state coolants at temperatures where collisional equilibrium would retain them. It can therefore suppress primordial line-cooling peaks. It also supplies photoionization heating. The net loss is cooling minus heating and depends on radiation spectrum, intensity, shielding and gas density. A universal density-independent function of temperature alone is not generally sufficient for irradiated gas.
Optically thin gas cooling time (tcool​=3χkB​T/(2nH​Λ))
Words: 117 Articles: 1
Astrophysical cooling function OurBigBook.com
For a nonrelativistic ideal gas with ntot​ thermal particles per volume, divide its thermal energy 3ntot​kB​T/2 by the optically thin volume radiation loss. In the nH2​ cooling convention this becomes 3χkB​T/(2nH​Λ), where χ=ntot​/nH​. Density scaling and ionization-dependent particle count must be kept consistent.
Cooling-to-free-fall equality curve (nH,crit​=3πXfg​32Gmp​​(2Λ3χkB​T​)2)
Words: 68
Optically thin gas cooling time OurBigBook.com
Equating the optically thin cooling time to the uniform-sphere free-fall time gives a critical gas density proportional to T2/Λ2. With hydrogen mass fraction X, particle ratio χ and gravitating gas fraction fg​, it is [32Gmp​/(3πXfg​)][3χkB​T/(2Λ)]2. At fixed temperature, gas above this density cools faster than free fall. A smaller gravitating gas fraction moves the boundary upward because gravity is faster at a fixed gas density.
Primordial atomic cooling curve (ΛH,He​(T))
Words: 46
Astrophysical cooling function OurBigBook.com
The primordial atomic cooling curve describes hydrogen-helium gas without heavy elements. Near the hydrogen excitation threshold it rises sharply, then shows hydrogen and helium excitation/ionization features. Bound-state losses weaken when both elements become highly ionized. At sufficiently high temperatures thermal bremsstrahlung gives a slowly rising tail. Composition, density convention and ionization assumptions fix the numerical normalization.
Atomic line cooling (Cline​=∑ne​ni​qij​(T)Eij​)
Words: 93 Articles: 1
Astrophysical cooling function OurBigBook.com
Atomic line cooling removes gas kinetic energy by collisional excitation followed by photon escape. It is strongest where atoms or ions have bound electrons and thermally accessible transitions. If photons are trapped, or if the relevant atoms are fully ionized, the simple optically thin line-cooling rate no longer gives the same loss.
Metal-line cooling (Λ(T,Z))
Words: 47
Atomic line cooling OurBigBook.com
Heavy elements provide many ionic transitions at temperatures where hydrogen and helium have lost their most effective line emitters. Metal-line cooling can therefore increase the plasma cooling function substantially and broaden its temperature features. Low-energy fine-structure transitions also permit cooling below the hydrogen atomic threshold when the relevant ions and electrons are present.

Heat flux density (q)

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Heat OurBigBook.com
Heat flux density is a vector q describing the rate of heat transfer per unit area, measured in Wm−2. Through a planar face of area A with uniform normal component q, the signed rate is Q˙​=Aq in W; positive q means heat travels in the chosen positive normal direction. Fourier's law determines the conductive contribution. In a bar with a constant cross-sectional area, steady thermal conduction without internal sources or side losses makes both q and Q˙​ constant along the bar. Constant Q˙​ need not mean constant q when the cross-sectional area varies.

Heat flow probe (q=kdT/dz)

Words: 43
Heat flux density OurBigBook.com
An instrument that combines subsurface temperature measurements with constraints on thermal conductivity to estimate a local heat flux. Multiple sensor depths help separate a stable geothermal gradient from surface-temperature transients and installation disturbance. Conductive heat flow can differ from total heat transport where fluid circulation carries substantial energy.

Thermal conduction

Words: 5k Articles: 31
Heat OurBigBook.com
Thermal conduction transfers heat through microscopic interactions without bulk transport of matter. To predict the heating load through a bar, combine Fourier's law with conservation of energy and the imposed end temperatures. In the isotropic model with positive thermal conductivity k, the conductive heat flux points from high to low temperature, opposite to the temperature gradient. A spoon warming along its handle and heat escaping through a wall are familiar examples.
Consider a bar of length L=0.10m, constant cross-sectional area A=0.010m2 and constant thermal conductivity k=2Wm−1K−1. Maintain its ends at Th​=40∘C and Tc​=20∘C, with x increasing toward the colder end. Assume a steady state, one-dimensional thermal conduction, no internal sources and no heat transfer through the sides. The temperature falls by 20K over 0.10m, giving
dxdT​=−200Km−1,q=−kdxdT​=400Wm−2,Q˙​=Aq=4W.
(4)
The difference between the two readings in degree Celsius units is the same 20-kelvin difference. The positive heat flux carries heat toward increasing x.
The general solution under these assumptions is
T(x)=Th​−LTh​−Tc​​x,q=Lk(Th​−Tc​)​,Q˙​=LkA(Th​−Tc​)​.
(5)
A proof outline is enough to explain the straight line: conservation of energy in any small slice, with no accumulation, sources or side losses, gives dQ˙​/dx=0. Constant cross-sectional area gives dq/dx=0; constant thermal conductivity and Fourier's law then give d2T/dx2=0. Two integrations and the end boundary conditions determine the displayed affine function. This is why a visually simple temperature profile can encode a continuous flow of energy. [ref]
Doubling the length halves the rate, while doubling the cross-sectional area doubles it, at fixed end temperatures and thermal conductivity. This explains why a long narrow support can limit unwanted heat transfer, while a short broad path can help remove heat. Joining materials leads to thermal resistance in series. During initial warming, internal energy can accumulate and the temperature profile need not be a straight line; the time dependence is described by the heat equation and thermal diffusivity.
Now join two layers, each of length L1​=L2​=0.10m, with constant cross-sectional area A=0.010m2 and stipulated constant thermal conductivities k1​=1 and k2​=4Wm−1K−1. Keep the outer ends at 40 and 20∘C. Assume a steady state, one-dimensional thermal conduction, no internal sources or side losses, and perfect contact: the temperature is continuous at the interface, with no extra contact drop. For each layer, use the area-specific thermal resistance ri​=Li​/ki​ and Ri​=ri​/A. The series calculation gives
r1​+r2​=k1​L1​​+k2​L2​​=0.100+0.025=0.125m2KW−1,R1​+R2​=Ar1​+r2​​=12.5KW−1,q=0.125m2KW−120K​=160Wm−2,Q˙​=Aq=1.6W,ΔT1​=qr1​=16K,ΔT2​=qr2​=4K,Tinterface​=40∘C−16K=24∘C.​
(6)
The heat flux is continuous: otherwise energy would accumulate at the interface. Yet Fourier's law gives different temperature gradients, dT/dx=−q/k1​=−160Km−1 and dT/dx=−q/k2​=−40Km−1. Lower thermal conductivity requires a steeper temperature gradient to carry the same heat flux; equal lengths therefore give drops in the ratio 4:1. A kink in the temperature profile records the change of material while perfect contact keeps the temperature itself continuous.

Entropy production by Fourier heat conduction (ρDtDS​=∇⋅Tk∇T​+T2k∣∇T∣2​)

Words: 93
Thermal conduction OurBigBook.com
For an ideal gas with specific internal energy cv​T and Fourier's law heat flux q=−k∇T, subtraction of the kinetic-energy balance from total energy gives ρcv​DT/Dt+p∇⋅u=∇⋅(k∇T). The thermodynamic entropy satisfies TDS/Dt=cv​DT/Dt+p∇⋅u/ρ, so
ρDtDS​=T1​∇⋅(k∇T)=∇⋅(Tk∇T​)+T2k∣∇T∣2​.
(7)
The divergence describes entropy transport by heat; the final term is local irreversible production. For T>0 and k≥0 it is nonnegative. In a fixed impermeable thermally insulated container, boundary entropy flux vanishes and mass conservation gives d∫ρSdV/dt=∫k∣∇T∣2/T2dV. Insulation conserves total energy while permitting entropy to increase as temperature gradients relax.

Steady heat conduction through layers (ΔT=q∑j​Lj​/kj​)

Words: 62
Thermal conduction OurBigBook.com
In one-dimensional steady heat conduction without internal heat sources, conservation of energy gives constant heat flux q=−kT′. Through a layer of thickness Lj​ and positive thermal conductivity kj​, the temperature drop is qLj​/kj​. If adjoining layers are in perfect thermal contact, temperature and heat flux are continuous at each interface, so summing the layer drops proves the displayed formula. Temperature is piecewise linear and its slope may jump when thermal conductivity changes.

Slab conduction with exponentially decaying heat generation (β=μa)

Words: 47
Thermal conduction OurBigBook.com
A one-dimensional thermal conduction model with constant thermal conductivity, source q′′′(x)=q0​e−μx and prescribed face temperatures T(0)=T(a)=T0​. Its steady state solution is

Fourier's law (q=−k∇T)

Words: 695 Articles: 6
Thermal conduction OurBigBook.com
Fourier's law predicts the local conductive heat flux from the local temperature gradient. In a continuum approximation with isotropic thermal conductivity k>0, its vector form and one-dimensional form are
q=−k∇T,q=−kdxdT​,Q˙​=Aqfor uniform normal flux over area A.
(10)
The heat flux q has units Wm−2, the temperature gradient has units Km−1 and the thermal conductivity has units Wm−1K−1. The rate of heat transfer Q˙​ has units W. These units distinguish a local material response from the total power crossing a surface.
The minus sign makes heat flow toward lower temperature: for k>0, q⋅∇T=−k∣∇T∣2≤0. In the worked bar in thermal conduction, dT/dx=−200Km−1 therefore gives q=+400Wm−2. Reversing the end temperatures reverses the heat flux. A zero temperature gradient gives zero conductive heat flux in this model.
Fourier's law is a constitutive relation expressing measured material behavior; it is not a consequence of conservation of energy alone. It applies locally and does not require a steady state. The straight-line bar solution additionally assumes constant thermal conductivity, constant cross-sectional area, no sources or side losses, and fixed end temperatures. Anisotropic materials require the directional response described by the thermal conductivity tensor. The scalar k used in the examples expresses the stated isotropy assumption. [ref]
Historically, Joseph Fourier's Théorie analytique de la chaleur was published in 1822. In Chapter II, article 112, he writes the heat crossing a spherical surface as the product of thermal conductivity, elapsed time, surface area and the negative radial temperature gradient; article 113 balances the incoming and outgoing heat to obtain the heat equation for a sphere. The enduring idea is this connection between a local flow rule and a global prediction of changing temperature. [ref] [ref]

Thermal conductivity is the material response coefficient in Fourier's law. For an isotropic material it is a scalar k, with units Wm−1K−1; larger positive k means a larger conductive heat flux for the same temperature gradient. It can depend on temperature and composition. Direction-dependent response in an anisotropic material is described by a thermal conductivity tensor. The two worked examples use stipulated positive constants, rather than measured values for named materials.
Thermal conductivity describes material response, whereas thermal resistance also includes geometry: for the steady bar, Rth​=L/(kA). Doubling k at fixed length, cross-sectional area and end temperatures halves thermal resistance and doubles the rate of heat transfer. Doubling length changes thermal resistance without changing the material's thermal conductivity. This distinction lets a designer improve cooling either by choosing a higher thermal conductivity or by shortening and widening the path. It also explains why the less conductive layer in thermal resistance takes the greater temperature drop.
Thermal diffusivity answers a different question: how rapidly a temperature disturbance spreads. Its usual model κ=k/(ρcp​) also involves mass density ρ and specific heat capacity cp​, so equal thermal conductivities need not imply equal rates of warming.

A material can carry substantial heat yet change temperature slowly because it stores substantial internal energy per kelvin.

A rigid fixed-volume model instead uses specific heat capacity at constant volume; a compressible moving fluid requires the accompanying work and transport terms. Thus the constraint is part of the approximation, not a choice made solely from the units. [ref]

Ångström periodic heating method

Words: 2k Articles: 6
Thermal diffusivity OurBigBook.com
The Ångström periodic heating method measures thermal diffusivity by periodically heating one end of a rod and comparing the resulting temperature oscillations at two separated thermometers. The farther signal has a smaller amplitude and a later wave phase. Their combination measures how quickly the material redistributes heat, without requiring the absolute heater power. The method bears the name of Anders Jonas Ångström, the physicist who became a professor at Uppsala in 1858.[ref]
An actual teaching apparatus is PASCO's TD-8513: four metal bars share a heater/cooler using the thermoelectric effect, and each has two embedded thermistors about 3cm apart. Foam covers reduce environmental heat transfer. Its manual instructs students to measure sensor spacing and connect the thermistors through a temperature interface to a computer. For the aluminium bar, a 0–8V triangular drive is applied with a 30s period. Recording begins after the amplitudes stabilize; two cycles provide amplitudes and the delay between corresponding peaks. Repeated runs at 40 and 50s test consistency. The manual converts the inferred thermal diffusivity to thermal conductivity using mass density and specific heat capacity.[ref]
For a general rod experiment, attach small thermocouples, thermistors or other thermometers at measured positions x1​<x2​, record both against the same clock, and establish a steady periodic thermal state. A sinusoid is especially convenient. For a switched or triangular drive, isolate the same Fourier series component at both sensors: unrelated peaks in distorted waveforms need not measure that component's phase difference. Subtract each sensor's mean temperature; a steady spatial background does not belong in the oscillating amplitude ratio. Small excursions help keep thermal conductivity, mass density and specific heat capacity constant.
The appeal is that the rod supplies two complementary clocks: decreasing amplitude measures spatial damping, while increasing wave phase lag measures delay. Unlike laser flash analysis, which follows a transient after one pulse, this method repeatedly samples a steady periodic thermal state. The timing determines thermal diffusivity α in m2s−1. To infer thermal conductivity k in Wm−1K−1, also measure or otherwise justify the mass density ρ and specific heat capacity at constant pressure cp​:
k=ρcp​α.
(15)
Here the stationary-solid approximation neglects thermal expansion and mechanical work, as in thermal diffusivity. A timing measurement alone cannot distinguish two materials with the same α and different volumetric heat capacities.

If a complex wavenumber K is defined by eiωt−iKx instead, K=b−ia.

The apparent phase velocity is ω/b=2αω​, which depends on frequency. A thermal diffusion wave therefore does not give a material-independent travel speed for heat; it is a forced pattern in a dissipative diffusion equation. Thermal diffusivity OurBigBook.com
Laser flash analysis measures thermal diffusivity by heating one face of a specimen briefly and recording the opposite face's temperature rise. The original 1961 experiment used a flash tube rather than a laser: a blackened thin metal specimen sat in an opaque ceramic holder, with thermocouple wires pressed against its rear face. An amplifier, oscilloscope and camera recorded the signal. Uniform front illumination and the black coating promoted uniform absorption; the opaque low-thermal conductivity holder blocked direct rear illumination and reduced edge losses. The delayed rear response reveals internal thermal conduction rather than direct heating of the sensor. [ref]
A modern version uses a laser or flash lamp, a specimen of measured thickness L, controlled initial temperature, and a rear-facing infrared detector with a synchronized recorder. The readout is a temperature rise versus time, starting from a pre-pulse baseline. Thermal conductivity additionally requires mass density and specific heat capacity; it is not obtained from timing alone. [ref]
Under ideal one-dimensional, insulated, constant-property assumptions, instantaneous uniform absorption in a very thin front layer gives the normalized rear rise
R(t)=T∞​−T0​T(L,t)−T0​​=1+2∑n=1∞​(−1)nexp(−L2n2π2αt​),t>0.
(28)
Here T0​ is the initial uniform temperature and T∞​ is the final uniform temperature in the insulated model. Fitting this curve estimates thermal diffusivity; each term has the same αKn2​ decay as the insulated-bar Fourier modes. Equivalently, the half-rise time t1/2​ solves R(t1/2​)=1/2. Writing s=αt/L2, the series gives s1/2​≈0.13879, hence
α≈0.13879t1/2​L2​.
(29)
This coefficient comes from the stated ideal heat equation solution, not from an empirical sensor calibration. It has been independently checked by solving the series equation. Absolute absorbed pulse energy cancels from the normalized curve; determining heat capacity from its absolute height needs additional information. [ref]
Parker and colleagues identify finite flash duration, heat loss, nonuniform illumination, recording bandwidth and electrical interference as practical limits. A specimen too thin responds during the pulse; one too thick allows losses before the rear rise finishes. They shielded the electrical chain and recorded a baseline; their reported tests were preliminary metal measurements near ambient and moderately elevated temperatures. [ref]
Useful additional controls are to measure thickness at several points, verify the recorder's time scale and detector response independently, record a no-pulse baseline, and repeat at different pulse energies while avoiding phase transitions. The Stefan–Boltzmann law gives the total hemispherical radiant exitance of an ideal blackbody at absolute temperature T:
Mb​(T)=σT4,[Mb​]=Wm−2.
(30)
Here σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. Total means integrated over all wavelengths; hemispherical means integrated over all outward directions with the projected area weighting. Thus Mb​ is emitted power per actual emitting area, rather than directional radiance or spectral radiance. Absolute temperature must be in kelvin; raising a Celsius reading to the fourth power gives the wrong result. A uniform surface of area A emits radiant flux Pemit​=AMb​. A real surface instead has M=ϵ(T)σT4, where ϵ(T) is its total hemispherical emissivity. The older symbol F in the formula above denotes this emitted radiant exitance.[ref]
For an ideal blackbody, doubling absolute temperature multiplies radiant exitance by 16. With the approximate Stefan-Boltzmann constant 5.670374419×10−8Wm−2K−4, the radiant exitances at 300K and 600K are approximately 459.300 and 7348.805Wm−2. This steep response explains why thermal radiation becomes so consequential at high temperature. It also enables heat transfer through a vacuum, where thermal conduction through a gas and convection are absent.
A short derivation integrates Planck's law in its frequency form. For a blackbody, direction-independent spectral radiance is Bν​(T)=2hν3/[c2(ehν/(kB​T)−1)], where h is the Planck constant, kB​ the Boltzmann constant and c the speed of light. The outward hemisphere contributes ∫cosθdΩ=π, so

Repeated integration by parts gives ∫0∞​x3e−nxdx=6/n4; the Riemann zeta function value ζ(4)=π4/90 gives the remaining integral as π4/15. Hence Mb​=σT4 with the coefficient in Stefan-Boltzmann constant. The angular integral is essential: omitting it confuses radiance with radiant exitance.

Emissivity (ϵ)

Emissivity compares thermal emission from a surface with emission from an ideal blackbody at the same absolute temperature, using the same wavelength and angular averaging convention. For ordinary passive surfaces in the far field at local thermal equilibrium, the ratio lies between zero and one. A blackbody has emissivity one. Unless a spectral or directional qualification is given, the ϵ in M=ϵσT4 is total hemispherical emissivity: a ratio of emitted radiant exitances, not of all outgoing radiant flux including reflected radiation.[ref]

A surface that looks white in visible light need not have low infrared emissivity. This distinction is useful when choosing a radiator coating or interpreting a radiation-based temperature measurement: a narrow-band detector needs the appropriate spectral emissivity, and its signal can include reflected surrounding radiation. The grey body and diffuse thermal emitter assumptions are separate simplifications, addressing wavelength and direction respectively.

Heat capacity measures the heat supplied per small temperature increase along a specified process:
CX​=(dTδQ​)X​.

The subscript X records the constraint, such as fixed volume or fixed pressure. The units are JK−1. The symbol δQ emphasizes that heat is a transfer along a path, rather than a state function with a differential dQ. Consequently, an unspecified heat capacity does not determine the required heat.
For a closed system of fixed composition undergoing a quasistatic process, assume that only pressure-volume work occurs, with no friction and no change in bulk kinetic energy or potential energy. The first law of thermodynamics and H=U+pV, where U is internal energy and H is enthalpy, then give

These partial derivatives define heat capacity at constant volume and heat capacity at constant pressure, with the amount and composition also held fixed. Integrating along the selected constraint gives Q=∫T1​T2​​CX​(T)dT within a single thermodynamic phase; Q=CX​ΔT requires constant CX​. [ref]
For a computed example, take a monatomic gas in the classical ideal gas regime, with amount of substance n=1mol and stipulated molar gas constant R=8.314Jmol−1K−1. The equipartition theorem gives U=3nRT/2, and the ideal gas law gives pV=nRT. Thus

For the same temperature increase ΔT=10K, the two processes require

Here work done by the gas is positive. At fixed pressure, the extra heat supplies expansion work; the internal energy increase is the same because internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature. Their final volume values differ. [ref]
The practical value of heat capacity is that a measured heat input and temperature response can determine it. Once its constraint and temperature dependence are known, it predicts heating requirements and supplies entropy changes through entropy from heat capacity. [ref]

Heat capacity OurBigBook.com
A Schottky anomaly is a peak in heat capacity caused by thermal occupation of a small set of separated energy levels. For N independent two-level units with equal degeneracies and gap Δ>0, write x=Δ/(kB​T); their heat capacity is C=NkB​x2e−x/(1+e−x)2, with Boltzmann constant kB​. It vanishes at both low and high temperature and can spoil a lattice T3 fit in between. Localized electronic or nuclear levels can contribute, including in calorimeter addenda; their presence must be checked rather than attributed automatically to phonons.

Schottky anomaly with unequal degeneracies (CV​/(NkB​)=x2g0​g1​e−x/(g0​+g1​e−x)2)

Words: 66
Schottky anomaly OurBigBook.com
For independent units with lower and upper energy levels separated by Δ>0, let their degeneracies be g0​ and g1​. Their shifted partition function is q=g0​+g1​e−x, with x=Δ/(kB​T). Differentiation gives
NkB​CV​​=x2(g0​+g1​e−x)2g0​g1​e−x​.
(52)
The heat capacity vanishes at both low and high temperature. Degeneracy changes both the maximum and its temperature; the equal-degeneracy result is not universal. Independent lower-level degeneracy also leaves residual entropy NkB​lng0​ in the ideal model.

Molar heat capacity (Cm​=C/n)

Words: 60
Heat capacity OurBigBook.com
Molar heat capacity is heat capacity divided by amount of substance n, with units Jmol−1K−1. Its constraint must still be specified: CV,m​=CV​/n and Cp,m​=Cp​/n. For the classical monatomic gas example in heat capacity, these are 3R/2 and 5R/2, where R is the molar gas constant. Some textbooks use CV​ and Cp​ for these per-mole quantities; the convention here reserves them for the whole sample.

Heating curve

Words: 46
Heat capacity OurBigBook.com
A heating curve records temperature against accumulated supplied heat under a specified constraint. Within one thermodynamic phase, its slope is dT/dQ=1/CX​, where CX​ is the constrained heat capacity. A latent heat plateau instead records changing phase fraction at the phase coexistence temperature. The sensible heat example combines two sloping intervals and a melting plateau in one heating budget.

Entropy from heat capacity

Words: 31
Heat capacity OurBigBook.com
Along a reversible path at fixed volume, dS=CV​(T)dT/T. Hence entropy differences can be measured macroscopically from
S(T2​)−S(T1​)=∫T1​T2​​TCV​(T)​dT,
(53)
with an additional L/Tc​ across a first-order transition of latent heat L at Tc​.

Entropy concavity and positive heat capacity

Words: 30
Heat capacity OurBigBook.com
For a thermodynamically stable system, the entropy is concave in energy, so
∂E2∂2S​=−T21​∂E∂T​<0.
(54)
Consequently ∂E/∂T>0: energy increases with temperature, and the corresponding heat capacity is positive.

Specific heat capacity (c=C/m)

Words: 338 Articles: 4
Heat capacity OurBigBook.com
Specific heat capacity is heat capacity per unit mass:
c=mC​,cV​=mCV​​,cp​=mCp​​.
(55)
Its units are Jkg−1K−1, and the constraint remains part of the definition. In particular, specific heat capacity at constant volume and specific heat capacity at constant pressure are different responses. For homogeneous material, doubling the mass doubles its heat capacity while leaving its specific heat capacity unchanged. [ref]
As an illustrative material model, give a fixed-volume body mass m=2kg and constant specific heat capacity at constant volume cV​=400Jkg−1K−1. With no phase transition and no other work, increasing its uniform temperature by 10K requires
CV​=mcV​=800JK−1,Q=mcV​ΔT=8000J=ΔU.
(56)
These stipulated values describe no measured substance. The right panel of the diagram in heat capacity shows the straight line Q=mcV​ΔT: a temperature increase of 5K takes 4000J of heat. If the specific heat capacity at constant volume depends on temperature, use Q=m∫T1​T2​​cV​(T)dT instead. The corresponding fixed-pressure calculation uses specific heat capacity at constant pressure and gives Q=ΔH under the assumptions in heat capacity.
Choosing between specific heat capacity, molar heat capacity and volumetric heat capacity is choosing whether to compare equal mass, equal amount of substance or equal volume. A small sample with large specific heat capacity can still have less total heat capacity than a much larger sample.

Volumetric heat capacity (Cvol​=C/V=ρc)

Words: 54
Specific heat capacity OurBigBook.com
Volumetric heat capacity is heat capacity per unit volume, with units Jm−3K−1. For homogeneous material of mass density ρ=m/V, it equals ρc, using specific heat capacity c for the same constraint. It measures the heat required per small temperature increase for a chosen occupied volume. In a material model using specific heat capacity at constant pressure, thermal diffusivity is α=k/(ρcp​), where k is thermal conductivity.

Specific heat capacity at constant volume (cV​=(∂u/∂T)ρ​)

Words: 30
Specific heat capacity OurBigBook.com
The specific heat capacity at constant volume is the temperature derivative of specific internal energy at fixed density and composition: cV​=(∂u/∂T)ρ​. It is the corresponding extensive heat capacity at constant volume divided by material mass.

Specific heat capacity at constant pressure (cP​)

Words: 92 Articles: 1
Specific heat capacity OurBigBook.com
The specific heat capacity at fixed pressure and composition is cP​=(∂h/∂T)P​, where h is specific enthalpy. Equivalently, it is heat capacity at constant pressure divided by mass. Under the process assumptions in heat capacity, it includes expansion work as well as the internal energy change. The sensible heat example uses this response separately for ice and water.
Pure-radiation constant-pressure heat-capacity singularity
Words: 49
Specific heat capacity at constant pressure OurBigBook.com
For pure blackbody radiation, P=aT4/3 depends only on temperature. Constant pressure therefore fixes temperature, so a usual finite constant-pressure temperature derivative is unavailable. In the material gas-radiation limit the specific-heat ratio diverges, although all three stellar adiabatic exponents approach 4/3. The radiation index 4/3 is an adiabatic pressure-volume response, not a finite heat-capacity ratio.

Heat capacity at constant volume (CV​)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Heat capacity OurBigBook.com
For a fixed-composition closed system, the heat capacity at fixed volume is CV​=(∂U/∂T)V​, with internal energy U. Under the quasistatic process assumptions in heat capacity, only pressure-volume work is permitted, so dV=0 gives δQ=dU=CV​dT. A rigid vessel therefore needs Q=ΔU, or Q=CV​ΔT when CV​ is constant. Its per-unit-mass counterpart is specific heat capacity at constant volume.

Temperature-linear pressure and volume-independent heat capacity ((∂CV​/∂V)T​=T(∂2p/∂T2)V​)

Words: 43
Heat capacity at constant volume OurBigBook.com
For a smooth simple compressible system, CV​=T(∂S/∂T)V​ and the Maxwell relation (∂S/∂V)T​=(∂p/∂T)V​ give (∂CV​/∂V)T​=T(∂2p/∂T2)V​. Thus an equation of state p=a(V)T+b(V) implies that CV​ depends on temperature alone within a smooth phase. It does not require CV​ to be temperature independent.

Dulong-Petit law

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Heat capacity at constant volume OurBigBook.com
In the classical high-temperature limit, each independent harmonic oscillator contributes kB​ to the heat capacity at constant volume, where kB​ is the Boltzmann constant. A three-dimensional crystalline solid with N chemical atoms has 3N vibrational normal modes in the bulk harmonic approximation. Its vibrational internal energy and heat capacity at constant volume therefore obey
Uvib​=U0​+3NkB​T,CV​=(∂T∂Uvib​​)V,N​=3NkB​.
(57)
Here U0​ is independent of temperature at fixed volume. Thus the Dulong-Petit law predicts CV​≃3NkB​ for a real solid in this regime. Per mole of chemical atoms, rather than per mole of a compound's formula units,
CV,mol​⟶3R≃24.9434Jmol−1K−1,R=NA​kB​,
(58)
with molar gas constant R and Avogadro constant NA​. A formula unit containing r chemical atoms consequently has a classical vibrational prediction of 3rR per mole of formula units.
For example, in this ideal classical model, one mole of chemical atoms heated at fixed volume from 300 to 600K gains vibrational internal energy
ΔUvib​=3R(600−300)K≃7483.02J.
(59)
The heat capacity at constant volume stays the same even though the thermal part of the internal energy doubles. These temperatures illustrate the stipulated classical model; they do not assert that every real solid is classical at 300K.
The proof outline is the equipartition theorem: one classical harmonic oscillator has a quadratic kinetic energy and a quadratic potential energy, each with mean kB​T/2. Their sum is kB​T, whose derivative with respect to temperature is kB​. Summing over 3N normal modes gives 3NkB​. The classical result does not require equal angular frequencies: each harmonic normal mode contributes the same amount once it is classical. Overall rigid motions give only a finite-size correction to the bulk count. This independence from the individual angular frequencies makes the Dulong-Petit law useful as a quick estimate of a solid's heating requirement.
Experiments on freely expanding solids often measure the heat capacity at constant pressure CP​, whereas the harmonic prediction is for the heat capacity at constant volume CV​. In a smooth single thermodynamic phase of a simple compressible material, the difference between constant-pressure and constant-volume heat capacities is
CP​−CV​=κT​TVα2​,
(60)
where α=V−1(∂V/∂T)P​ is the volumetric coefficient of thermal expansion and κT​=−V−1(∂V/∂P)T​ is the isothermal compressibility. Using measured CP​ as an approximation to CV​ requires this correction to be small compared with CV​. [ref]
High temperature here means kB​T≫ℏω for the relevant vibrational normal modes, with reduced Planck constant ℏ and mode angular frequency ω. At low temperature, excitation across a quantum energy spacing is suppressed: modes with ℏω≫kB​T freeze out thermally, and the classical equipartition theorem fails. The Einstein model of a solid makes this loss of vibrational heat capacity explicit. The Dulong-Petit law is therefore an ideal high-temperature vibrational limit, not a statement that all solids have the same heat capacity at every temperature. Other contributions and departures from the harmonic approximation can matter even at high temperature. [ref]
Historically, Petit and Dulong's 1819 experiments compared the specific heat capacities of several elemental solids and found an approximately constant product with their relative atomic weights. Their original empirical regularity came before the classical harmonic explanation; it suggested that counting chemical atoms reveals a simpler pattern than comparing equal masses. [ref]
Einstein solid (CV​/(3NkB​)=x2ex/(ex−1)2)
Words: 578 Articles: 2
Dulong-Petit law OurBigBook.com
The Einstein model of a solid represents the vibrations of N chemical atoms by 3N independent one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillators, all with the same positive angular frequency ω. Equivalently, each chemical atom has three independent oscillator directions. The common angular frequency is a simplifying model assumption, not a claim about every vibration of a real solid. Hold the volume, N and ω fixed. Define the characteristic temperature θE​=ℏω/kB​ and the dimensionless ratio x=θE​/T. The vibrational internal energy is
U=3Nℏω[21​+ex−11​],x=kB​Tℏω​=TθE​​.
(61)
The first term is the zero-point energy 3Nℏω/2. It is constant at fixed ω, so it contributes no heat capacity at constant volume. The temperature-dependent term gives
3NkB​CV​​=(ex−1)2x2ex​=(1−e−x)2x2e−x​.
(62)
This is the vibrational heat capacity at constant volume of the model, with no expansion or other contributions included. [ref]
For a worked comparison, choose the model parameter θE​=300K. The normalized heat capacity at constant volume depends only on T/θE​:
T/θE​Temperature T in KCV​/(3NkB​)
0.1300.00454
0.51500.72406
13000.92067
26000.97942
At T=θE​, one mole of chemical atoms therefore has vibrational heat capacity at constant volume 3R(0.92067)≃22.965Jmol−1K−1, using the unrounded model value. Even at twice the characteristic temperature, the model remains about 2.06% below the Dulong-Petit law limit. These are calculations for the ideal Einstein solid, not material measurements.
A short derivation uses the thermal partition function of a quantum harmonic oscillator. The energy eigenvalues En​=ℏω(n+1/2) and their Boltzmann factors form a geometric series, giving the one-oscillator canonical partition function z=e−x/2/(1−e−x). The mean occupation is 1/(ex−1), hence the displayed U after summing over 3N independent quantum harmonic oscillators. Taking its derivative with dx/dT=−x/T gives the displayed heat capacity at constant volume. [ref]
The two limits explain the shape. At high temperature, a Taylor series in small x gives
3NkB​CV​​=1−12x2​+O(x4)⟶1(T≫θE​).
(63)
At low temperature, 1−e−x→1, so
3NkB​CV​​∼x2e−x⟶0(T≪θE​).
(64)
The zero-point energy remains even when the thermal response is tiny: freeze-out means that changing temperature scarcely changes the occupations, not that the chemical atoms have zero energy. This is the useful lesson of the Einstein model of a solid: the classical counting rule reappears when many levels are accessible, while discrete excitation spacings explain its failure upon cooling.
The exponential low-temperature decay is also the model's limitation. Real three-dimensional crystalline solids have acoustic phonon branches with arbitrarily small angular frequencies in the bulk limit. The Debye model includes these collective normal modes and predicts a low-temperature vibrational contribution CV​∝T3, which the single-frequency Einstein solid cannot reproduce. This qualification concerns the vibrational contribution; additional excitations can change a material's total heat capacity. [ref]
Einstein introduced the quantum treatment of solid vibrations in his 1907 paper Die Plancksche Theorie der Strahlung und die Theorie der spezifischen Wärme. Its historical importance is that quantum excitation energies explained why the classical Dulong-Petit law could fail; the modern quantum harmonic oscillator formulation above includes the zero-point energy explicitly. [ref]
Einstein mean-square displacement (⟨x2⟩=ℏcoth(TE​/(2T))/(2mωE​))
Words: 51
Einstein solid OurBigBook.com
For one Cartesian direction in an Einstein solid, ⟨x2⟩=ℏ[2⟨n⟩+1]/(2mωE​). Substituting the thermal oscillator occupation proves the displayed result. At T≫TE​, equipartition gives ⟨x2⟩=kB​T/(mωE2​)=ℏ2T/(mkB​TE2​). The total displacement variance of an isotropic atom is three times the one-coordinate result, a distinction that matters in applying a melting threshold.
Einstein high-temperature heat-capacity expansion (CV​=3NkB​[1−TE2​/(12T2)+O(T−4)])
Words: 43
Einstein solid OurBigBook.com
Expanding the Einstein model of a solid internal energy gives U=3NkB​[T+TE2​/(12T)+O(T−3)], because the constant term in the thermal occupation cancels the zero-point energy. Differentiation yields the displayed heat capacity and proves absence of a 1/T term. The ratio of the T−2 and constant coefficients determines TE​ independently of sample size.

Heat capacity at constant area (CA​)

Words: 37
Heat capacity OurBigBook.com
For a two-dimensional system of fixed area A, the heat capacity at constant area is CA​=(∂E/∂T)N,A​ when the particle number and other conserved quantities are also fixed. It is the two-dimensional analogue of heat capacity at constant volume.

Electron heat capacity

Words: 29
Heat capacity OurBigBook.com
The contribution of electrons to heat capacity. For a uniform noninteracting three-dimensional Fermi gas at fixed particle number and volume, its low-temperature value is CV​≃(π2/2)NkB​T/TF​; only states near the Fermi surface can change occupation readily.
